memory_verse.label: Bible Reference
memory_verse.text: "Joseph said to the people, 'Now that I have bought you and your land today for Pharaoh, here is seed for you so you can plant the ground. But when the crop comes in, give a fifth of it to Pharaoh. The other four-fifths you may keep as seed for the fields and as food for yourselves and your households and your children.'" — Gen 47:23-24 (NIV)

devotion.label: Devotion
devotion.text:
Look carefully at the arrangement. A fifth to Pharaoh, four-fifths for the people. In an age when conquered populations could be stripped bare, a twenty percent tax is remarkably moderate — and the people will call it fair in the very next verses.

Notice also that Joseph gives them seed. He does not simply feed them; he puts them back to work. Handing someone a meal keeps them alive today. Handing them seed restores their dignity and their future.

That is a good pattern for anyone who wants to help others well. The kindest help usually aims at restoration, not dependence. Paul worked with his own hands so as not to burden anyone, and taught that those who can work should (2 Thess 3:10-12) — not harshly, but because work is part of how God made us to live.

If you are in a position to help someone, ask what would genuinely put them back on their feet. Sometimes that is a meal. Often it is seed.

And notice the hopefulness of the whole scene. Seed means the famine will end. Somebody is planning for a harvest again. God's seasons of scarcity do not last forever.

reflection.label: Reflection
reflection.text:
1. When you help others, do you aim at relief or at restoration?
2. Who around you might need seed rather than just a meal?
3. Where do you need to believe that this hard season will end?

prayer.label: Prayer
prayer.text: Father, teach me to help people in ways that restore them rather than keep them dependent. And where I am in a lean season, give me hope that You bring harvests again. Amen.
